title: Process Injection: Process Doppelgänging
summary: Process doppelgaenging abuses Windows Transactional NTFS, a file interface that stages changes inside a transaction and rolls them back on failure, to load malicious code without ever committing a malicious file to disk. The attacker opens a legitimate executable inside a transaction, overwrites the transacted view with payload data, creates a section from that transacted file, and then rolls the transaction back so the committed file on disk is unchanged. A process is created from the section, so the transacted image is what gets mapped and executed while the file on disk still looks completely legitimate. Because the approach avoids the image unmap and thread context rewrite calls that hollowing relies on, it sidesteps many injection detections. Defenders look for process creation from transacted file handles, image loads with no corresponding committed file, unusual transactional file activity, and running images that match nothing on disk.

beginner.definition: Process doppelgaenging hides malicious code by using a temporary, invisible copy of a real program. Windows can change a file inside something called a transaction, which works like a draft. The attacker edits the draft, uses it to start a process, and then discards it. The real file on disk never changes, so the computer looks clean.
beginner.whyItMatters: Many defences are built around files, because they scan downloads and check signatures. This technique means the harmful code may never exist as a file. The attacker's code runs inside a process that appears normal. Any trust decision based on the program name is therefore wrong. It also avoids the system calls that older detection rules watch most closely.
howItWorks: The attacker opens a real executable inside a Windows transaction, which is a reversible file operation.
While the transaction stays open, the contents of that file view are replaced with malicious code.
Other programs still see the original committed version, so nothing appears wrong at this point.
The attacker creates a memory section from the transacted file view, preparing an image to run.
The transaction is rolled back, so the original file on disk is left completely unchanged.
A process is started from the prepared section, and the hidden code runs under a trusted name.
beginner.example: Imagine a quiet library reading room on a weekday afternoon. A visitor asks for a rare book, and the librarian hands over a working copy for editing. The visitor replaces the text inside that copy with something else. Then he reads from the changed copy at the desk. When he leaves, the librarian throws the working copy away. The original book then returns to the shelf untouched. Tomorrow the catalogue still lists the same book, and the shelf copy looks perfect. Nothing on the shelves changed, yet the words read were not the words in the book.
takeaways: Harmful code can run even when no harmful file exists on the disk.
The technique reuses a real executable's identity, so names prove very little.
Ask whether a running image matches any file that was properly committed.

objectives: Explain in simple terms how Transactional NTFS lets file changes be rolled back.
Describe the transact, overwrite, section, rollback and create sequence.
Explain how this sub-technique differs from process hollowing.
Identify detection opportunities when a process starts from a transacted file.
Explain why file scanning alone cannot catch this technique.
